what_its_for: Tiopronin is used to prevent kidney stones made of a substance called cystine. It works by binding to cystine in your urine to help break it down so it can pass out of your body without forming painful stones. It is used in people who still form kidney stones even after trying other measures like drinking more water and changing their diet.
how_to_take: Take tiopronin by mouth with a full glass of water. You may take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help reduce stomach upset. If you are taking the regular tablets, try to take them at evenly spaced times throughout the day (usually 3 times a day). If you are taking the delayed-release tablets (Thiola EC), swallow them whole — do not crush, chew, or split them. Drink plenty of fluids throughout the day (at least 8 to 10 glasses of water daily) to help prevent kidney stones.
dosing: The usual starting dose for adults is 800 mg per day, split into 3 doses (about 267 mg each time). Your doctor may adjust your dose based on how much cystine is in your urine. For children, the starting dose is usually based on body weight (about 15 mg per kilogram per day), divided into 3 doses. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store tiopronin at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep it out of the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of the reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine past the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid becoming dehydrated — drink plenty of fluids every day. Avoid high-sodium (salty) foods and high-protein diets, as these can make cystine stones worse. Avoid alcohol in large amounts, as it can affect how well this medicine works and may harm your kidneys. Do not stop taking tiopronin without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel well.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you experience: fever, chills, or signs of infection; skin rash, blistering, or peeling; mouth sores; unusual bruising or bleeding; swollen glands; muscle weakness or joint pain; blood in your urine; signs of a kidney stone such as severe back or side pain, pain when urinating, or nausea and vomiting; signs of a serious allergic reaction such as trouble breathing, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); or any new or worsening symptoms that concern you.
when_it_works: Tiopronin starts working to lower cystine levels in your urine within a few weeks, but it may take several months before you notice a reduction in kidney stone formation. Your doctor will check your urine regularly to make sure the medicine is working. It is important to keep taking it every day as prescribed, even if you feel fine.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Tiopronin may harm an unborn baby and it is not known if it passes into breast milk, so the risks and benefits must be discussed with your doctor. Children: Tiopronin can be used in children, but the dose will be adjusted based on your child's weight. Children should be monitored closely by their doctor. Older adults: Older patients may be more sensitive to side effects. Your doctor may monitor you more closely. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have any kidney or liver problems before starting this medicine, as your dose may need to be adjusted.
